summary: Describes an architectural framework for controlling media servers. It defines the logical entities involved, their naming conventions, and how they interact. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5567 describes how an application server can direct a media server that plays, mixes, or records audio and video. SIP establishes separate media and control interactions between the systems.

subtitle: An architecture for application servers to control media servers with SIP

tldr.problem: Applications need to direct media servers, but an architecture was needed to describe the roles and their interactions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5567 describes application servers, media servers, SIP media and control dialogs, and the reliable channel used for control messages.
tldr.outcome: The Informational document provides an architectural framework for interactive voice and conferencing services; it does not define the media-control protocol itself.

facts.label: TLS implementation
facts.value: Required; use in deployments is optional

today: RFC 5567 is an Informational architecture document published in June 2009. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Application and Media Servers
sections.content:
An Application Server (AS) runs communication applications and decides how a service should work. A Media Server (MS) processes media streams, for example by playing announcements, mixing audio or video, detecting telephone key tones, or recording.

The RFC defines the logical roles and their interactions. An AS may control one or more media servers, and a media server may be controlled by more than one application server.
sections.plainLanguage: The application server decides what service a caller receives. The media server performs the requested work on audio and video streams.

sections.title: Separate Media and Control Dialogs
sections.content:
The AS uses SIP to establish both media sessions and control channels with the MS. The MS Media Dialog sets up the media session; the MS Control Dialog establishes a reliable channel for control messages.

Media streams flow directly between user agents and the media server. The control channel carries commands from the AS, responses from the MS, and notifications about results or events.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP sets up one interaction for the media and another for control. The media server sends and receives media while the application server issues instructions.

sections.title: Interactive Voice and Conferencing
sections.content:
A simple announcement can be requested without a mid-call control channel. More complex interactive voice response (IVR) services use control messages to play prompts, detect keypad or speech input, and report events such as a completed recording.

For a conference, the AS manages the media mix and may add or remove participants, adjust streams, or control video layout. The framework also describes floor control, where the system grants a participant permission to send media to a shared resource.
sections.plainLanguage: A basic service can play an announcement. More complex services let the application server respond to caller input or manage how conference participants' media is mixed.

sections.title: Reliable Control and Message Types
sections.content:
The control channel carries commands, responses, and notifications between an application server and a media server. The architecture requires reliable, sequenced delivery for these control messages.

Implementations must support TCP and may support SCTP. They must implement TLS as a transport-level security mechanism, although using TLS in a deployment is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: Control messages must arrive reliably and in order. Implementations must support TLS, though a deployment may choose whether to use it.

sections.title: Security and Resource Protection
sections.content:
Media servers are valuable resources and should accept control requests only from authorized application servers. SIP security mechanisms authenticate requests and protect their integrity, while TLS protects the control channel's messages.

A media server may serve multiple application servers. It must prevent one server from accessing or changing resources assigned to another; one approach is to associate each resource with the application server that allocated it.
sections.plainLanguage: Only authorized application servers should control media resources. The media server must keep each application's sessions separate.
